objectives: Given an activation code or your clinic's official sign-up link, create your patient portal account and sign in safely, using the official site or app, a password used nowhere else and two-step verification if offered

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting into your patient portal
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create your portal account and sign in safely.
This lesson builds toward: Given an activation code or your clinic's official sign-up link, you will create your patient portal account and sign in safely, using the official site or app, a password used nowhere else and two-step verification if offered.
A patient portal is a secure website or app from your clinic, hospital or health plan. Common ones include MyChart, used by many health systems, but your clinic's portal may have another name. Ask the front desk which portal they use.
To join, you usually need an activation code from the clinic (printed on a visit summary or sent by text or email) or you sign up with your name, date of birth and a code sent to your phone. Use the link on your clinic's official website or the official app from the app store.
Choose a strong password you do not use anywhere else, and turn on two-step verification if offered. Do not sign in on a shared computer unless you sign out and close the browser afterward.
Step by step:
- Ask your clinic which portal it uses.
- Get your activation code or sign-up link from the clinic.
- Use the clinic's official website or the official app.
- Create a strong, unique password.
- Turn on two-step verification if offered.
- On a shared computer: sign out and close the browser.
Words to know:
- Patient portal: a secure website or app where you see your health information and contact your care team.
- Activation code: a one-time code from your clinic that links your portal account to your records.
- Care team: your doctor, nurses and other staff who look after your health.
Try it now: Find your clinic's portal from its official website or ask the front desk. Create your account or sign in, then sign out and back in to be sure you can do it alone.
You can now find your clinic's patient portal, create your account and sign in safely.

check.q: Who can tell you which patient portal your clinic uses?
options: A search engine ad
A stranger online
Your bank
The clinic's front desk
check.why: Ask the front desk which portal the clinic uses.

check.q: You signed in to your portal on a library computer. What would you do when you finish?
options: Leave the page open for later
Sign out and close the browser
Save your password in the browser
Write your password on the desk
check.why: On a shared computer, sign out and close the browser afterwards.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reading test results and visit notes
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a test result and a visit summary in your portal.
This lesson builds toward: In your patient portal, you will find a test result and a visit summary and write down any question about them, reading the result next to its reference range and taking questions to your care team instead of guessing.
Portals have sections such as Test Results, Visits or Appointments, Medications and Health Summary. Results often show your number next to a normal or reference range. A result outside the range is often marked, but it does not always mean something is wrong.
You may see a result before your doctor has talked to you about it. Do not panic, and do not guess. Write down your question and ask your care team. An AI tool can help explain a medical word in simple language, but never type your name, date of birth or record numbers into it, and check its answer with your care team.
HealthIT.gov explains that, under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, you have the right to see and get a copy of your health record, including electronic copies, even if you have not paid your medical bills.
Step by step:
- Open Test Results or Results.
- Tap a result to see your number and the normal range.
- Open Visits to read your visit summary.
- Write down any word or result you do not understand.
- Ask your care team; do not guess.
Words to know:
- Reference range: the usual range of results for healthy people.
- Visit summary: notes from your appointment, like your plan and medicines.
- HIPAA: a US law that protects your health information and gives you the right to see your records.
Official sources:
- HealthIT.gov: How to get your health record
Try it now: In your portal, open one test result or visit summary. Write down one word or number you would like explained, to ask your care team.
You can now find and read a test result and visit summary, and know when to ask your care team.

check.q: What does a result outside the reference range mean?
options: It is not always a problem; ask your care team
You definitely have a serious illness
The test was done wrong
You should stop all your medicines
check.why: A marked result does not always mean something is wrong; ask your care team.

check.q: Your doctor has not seen your new results yet and you are worried. What would you do?
options: Guess what it means from a forum
Type your name and record number into an AI tool
Write down your question and ask your care team
Change your medicines yourself
check.why: Do not panic or guess; write down your question and ask your care team.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Messaging your care team
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Send a short, clear message to your care team through the portal.
This lesson builds toward: Given a non-urgent health question, you will write a short, clear portal message to your care team, with your question and helpful details, and with anything urgent sent to 911 instead.
Most portals have a Messages section for questions that are not urgent, like a question about a medicine, a form, or a result. Answers can take a day or more, so do not use messages for anything urgent. For an emergency, call 911.
A good message is short. Say who it is for, your question, and any details that help: when it started, what you have tried, and what you need. For example: "Since Monday I feel dizzy after my new blood pressure pill in the morning. Should I take it at night instead?"
Some clinics may bill your insurance for messages that need medical advice. Ask your clinic if you are not sure. Messages in the portal are secure; do not send health details by regular email or text instead.
Step by step:
- Open Messages and choose New message.
- Pick who it is for or the topic.
- Write your question, when it started and what you need.
- Read it once and send.
- Check the portal or your email for the reply.
- Urgent? Call the clinic. Emergency? Call 911.
Words to know:
- Secure message: a private message sent inside the portal.
- Non-urgent: can safely wait a day or two for an answer.
Try it now: Open Messages in your portal and draft a short message using the three parts. If you have a real non-urgent question, send it; if not, delete the draft.
You can now write and send a clear, non-urgent message to your care team, and know when to call instead.

check.q: Why should portal messages not be used for urgent problems?
options: Messages are not secure
Messages are always read by a robot
Answers can take a day or more
Messages cost money every time
check.why: Replies can take a day or more, so emergencies need 911.

check.q: You have a question about a form your clinic gave you. What would you do?
options: Send a short portal message saying what the form is and what you need
Send your health details by regular email
Call 911
Post the question on social media
check.why: Non-urgent questions go in a short, clear portal message.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Refills, appointments and video visits

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Requesting refills and booking appointments
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Request a medicine refill and find where to book or change an appointment.
This lesson builds toward: In your patient portal, you will request a medicine refill and find where to book or change an appointment, requesting the refill a few days before you run out and calling the clinic when the portal cannot do it.
In the Medications section, many portals show a Request refill button next to each medicine. Choose the medicine and your pharmacy, and send. Ask a few days before you run out, because the clinic and pharmacy need time.
In the Appointments or Visits section, you can often see upcoming visits, book some kinds of visits, cancel, or get on a waitlist. Some appointments must be booked by phone; the portal will say so.
Your pharmacy may have its own app that tells you when a refill is ready. If something does not work in the portal, call the clinic; that is always fine.
Step by step:
- Open Medications.
- Tap Request refill next to the medicine.
- Choose your pharmacy and send.
- Ask a few days before you run out.
- Open Appointments to see, book, change or cancel visits.
Words to know:
- Refill: more of a medicine you already take.
- Waitlist: a list that offers you an earlier time if someone cancels.
Try it now: Open the Medications section in your portal and find the refill button (send a request only if you need one). Then open Appointments and find your next visit or where to book one.
You can now request a refill and find, book or change an appointment in your portal.

check.q: Where do many portals show a Request refill button?
options: In the Test Results section
Next to each medicine in the Medications section
In the Messages inbox
On the sign-in page
check.why: Many portals put a refill button next to each medicine.

check.q: The portal's refill button does not work for one of your medicines. What would you do?
options: Stop taking the medicine
Wait until you run out
Order the medicine from a website ad
Call the clinic
check.why: If something does not work in the portal, calling the clinic is always fine.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting ready for a video visit
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Prepare your device, space and questions before a video visit.
This lesson builds toward: The day before a video visit, you will prepare your device, space, questions and medicine list, with the device charged, camera and microphone tested, and a written list ready.
A video visit (also called telemedicine or telehealth) lets you see a doctor, nurse or counselor on your phone, tablet or computer. It works well for many follow-ups, medicine checks, mental health visits and simple problems. Some problems still need an in-person exam, and your care team will tell you.
Get ready the day before: charge your device, make sure the portal app or video app is installed, and test your camera and microphone. Many portals have a test button or an eCheck-in you can do ahead of time.
Find a quiet, private, well-lit spot. Write down your questions, your symptoms and when they started, and a list of your medicines. Have your glasses, pill bottles and, if helpful, a blood pressure reading or thermometer nearby. A family member or caregiver can join to help if you want.
Step by step:
- Charge your device and check the app is installed.
- Test the camera and microphone.
- Do any eCheck-in in the portal.
- Choose a quiet, private, well-lit spot.
- Write your questions, symptoms and medicines.
- Keep pill bottles and glasses nearby.
Words to know:
- Telemedicine or telehealth: seeing your care team by video or phone instead of in person.
- eCheck-in: filling in forms in the portal before your visit.
Try it now: Write a list for your next visit: three questions, your symptoms and when they started, and every medicine you take with the dose. Keep it with your device.
You can now get your device, space and questions ready for a video visit.

check.q: Which kind of visit often works well by video?
options: A medicine check or follow-up
An emergency
A visit that needs an in-person exam
Surgery
check.why: Video visits work well for many follow-ups, medicine checks and counseling.

check.q: Your video visit is tomorrow and you are not sure your camera works. What would you do today?
options: Wait and see during the visit
Cancel the visit
Test the camera and microphone, using the portal's test button if it has one
Ask the clinic to visit your home
check.why: Testing the day before gives you time to fix a problem.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Joining and finishing a video visit
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Join a video visit on time, talk clearly and know the next steps.
This lesson builds toward: On the day of a video visit, you will join on time, talk clearly and repeat the plan back before you hang up, joining 10 to 15 minutes early and checking the visit summary afterwards.
Join 10 to 15 minutes early. Open the appointment in your portal and tap the button to begin the video visit, or use the link the clinic sent you. Allow the camera and microphone when asked. You may wait in a virtual waiting room until the clinician joins.
During the visit, look at the screen, speak clearly and use your list. If the sound or video drops, stay calm; the clinician will usually call you back, so keep your phone nearby. It is fine to ask them to repeat or explain something simply.
Before you hang up, repeat the plan back: "So I will take the new pill at night, and come back in two weeks?" Afterwards, check the portal for the visit summary and any new prescriptions or tests.
Step by step:
- Join 10 to 15 minutes early from the portal or the clinic's link.
- Allow camera and microphone.
- Wait in the virtual waiting room.
- Use your list; ask them to explain simply if needed.
- Repeat the plan back before you hang up.
- Read the visit summary in the portal afterwards.
Words to know:
- Virtual waiting room: a screen where you wait until the clinician joins.
- Clinician: a doctor, nurse, physician assistant or counselor who treats you.
Try it now: Final task practice: in your portal, open an upcoming or past appointment and find where the video visit button or link appears. Then do the final task: a result, a message, refills and appointments, and your visit list.
You can now join a video visit on time, talk through your list, confirm the plan and find the summary afterwards.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Signing in safely Cannot sign in, or signed in from an unofficial link. Signs in through the clinic's official site or app with a password used nowhere else. Also turns on two-step verification if the portal offers it. Finding a result or summary Cannot find a test result or visit summary. Finds one test result or visit summary and notes any question about it. Also reads the result against its reference range without guessing what it means. Clear message The message is unclear, long, or about something urgent. A short message with the question and helpful details, for a non-urgent need. Includes when it started, what was tried and what is needed. Refills and appointments Cannot find where to request a refill or appointment. Finds both the refill request and the appointment section. Also knows which appointments must be booked by phone. Ready for the video visit No question list or medicine list, or cannot say where the link will appear. Three questions and a current medicine list, and knows where the video link will appear. Also tests the camera and microphone or completes eCheck-in ahead of time. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where can you usually start a video visit?
options: From a link in a random text
From the appointment in your portal, or the link the clinic sent
From a search engine ad
From your bank's app
check.why: Open the appointment in your portal or use the clinic's link.

check.q: The doctor explains a new plan quickly near the end of the visit. What would you do?
options: Hang up and guess later
Ask a neighbor what the doctor meant
Say nothing to save time
Ask them to explain simply, then repeat the plan back
check.why: Repeating the plan back makes sure you understood the next steps.
